Band Neutrophil.text: Band neutrophils are associated with conditions involving a left shift, such as severe infections, inflammation, burns, and leukemoid reactions [2][4]. On a peripheral blood film, toxic changes like toxic granulation, vacuolation, and dohle bodies may be observed in neutrophils, including bands, indicating toxicity and an active response to infection or inflammation [1][4].

Basophil.text: Basophils are associated with conditions such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where marked basophilia is a pathognomonic feature and a prognostic factor [3][7]. They may also be involved in allergic responses, asthma, COPD, and other inflammatory or neoplastic hematologic disorders [1][5][6]. On a peripheral blood film, findings can include increased basophil count, sometimes with immature cells in cases of disease progression, and may be accompanied by other abnormal blood cell populations depending on the condition [6][7].

Eosinophil.text: Eosinophils are associated with a variety of conditions, including hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), allergic diseases like asthma and atopic dermatitis, parasitic infections, and certain cancers [1][8]. On a peripheral blood film, eosinophilia is indicated by an increased number or percentage of eosinophils, with counts above 0.5×10^9/L considered elevated and ≥1.5×10^9/L classified as hypereosinophilia [2][6]. The presence of eosinophil infiltrates or granule protein aggregates can also be observed, especially when associated with tissue pathology [7].

Lymphocyte.text: Lymphocytes are associated with reactive processes such as infections and inflammation, as well as neoplastic lymphoproliferative disorders [1][2]. In COVID-19, abnormal lymphocytes may appear as atypical, reactive, activated, or pleomorphic cells, similar to those seen in viral infections like EBV and CMV [2]. The presence of atypical or abnormal lymphocytes on a peripheral blood film can indicate a reactive or potentially malignant process, with morphological features varying depending on the underlying condition [2][3].

On a peripheral blood film, findings may include monocytosis, which is an elevated monocyte count, and in cases like COVID-19, monocyte vacuolization or atypical monocytes may be observed [4][6]. These morphological changes can reflect the body's response to inflammation or infection.

Segmented Neutrophil.text: Segmented neutrophils are associated with sepsis and inflammatory responses, often showing toxic granulations due to increased microbicidal granules [4][8]. On a peripheral blood film, these neutrophils may exhibit morphological abnormalities such as toxic granules, vacuolations, and hypersegmentation, especially in conditions like megaloblastic anemia or severe infections [4][8]. The presence of toxic granulations indicates active infection or inflammation, while hypersegmentation can be linked to other hematological conditions [8].

Monocyte|vacuolated.text: Monocytes are associated with inflammatory conditions such as atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and infections, and can be elevated in acute and chronic inflammatory states, including monocytosis [3][5]. On peripheral blood films, monocytes may show variable nuclear shapes, loose chromatin, and blue-gray ground glass cytoplasm that may contain pseudopods or vacuoles [1]. Cytoplasmic vacuolation in monocytes can be associated with reactive or infectious processes, and in COVID-19, it has been linked to milder disease and shorter hospital stays [4].

Cytoplasmic vacuolation in neutrophils suggests phagocytosis or autophagocytosis, often indicating an active response to infection or inflammation [8]. These vacuoles may contain bacteria or yeast if the patient is septic, reflecting the cell's role in host defense.
